transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Integrated risk prediction, for Wednesday, November 25.
Let's turn to integrated risk prediction, with two UK Biobank studies that pair polygenic scores with clinical information.
The first is from the Fahed lab in Frontiers in Neurology. It asks whether traumatic brain injury raises later cardiometabolic risk on its own, or only reflects inherited susceptibility.

Among about 487 thousand participants, 4,309 had an incident brain injury, which the authors modeled as a time-varying exposure in Cox models. Injury was independently associated with coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.
The joint effects of injury and polygenic scores were largely additive. Among survivors, outcome-specific scores were associated with every outcome, most strongly for coronary disease and diabetes.
A combined cardiometabolic meta-score had a hazard ratio of 1.19 for post-injury risk in UK Biobank. It replicated in the Mass General Brigham Biobank with a hazard ratio of 1.15.
The external replication is reassuring. Still, the injured group is only a few thousand people and the effect sizes are modest.

The second paper, from the He lab in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, combines a coronary polygenic score with the estimated glucose disposal rate. That's an insulin-resistance marker built from waist circumference, hypertension and hemoglobin A1c.

The authors studied both first and recurrent coronary disease over a median follow-up of 13.8 years. People with the highest glucose disposal rate and a low polygenic score had the lowest risk, with hazard ratios of 0.25 for incident and 0.67 for recurrent disease.
The two factors also interacted for incident disease. But adding both to conventional risk factors raised the C-index by only 0.017 for incident and 0.005 for recurrent disease.
So the gain in prediction is small, and since both studies rely mainly on UK Biobank, it's worth testing them in other cohorts.
Our takeaway: polygenic scores add consistent but modest information on top of clinical factors, whether the added risk comes from a brain injury or from insulin resistance.

papers.title: Genetic susceptibility and risk of cardiometabolic diseases after traumatic brain injury
Estimated Glucose Disposal Rate, Genetic Susceptibility and Risks of Incident and Recurrent Coronary Artery Disease: Evidence From the UK Biobank Study
